answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and only one decision available. A vendor switch (memory_c2) is the most tempting on unit cost but is the only option that injects qualification and onboarding risk into a period with zero slack \u2014 memory_c2 also reports cost and invoicing outcomes, not delivery performance under load, so it does not actually speak to the risk that matters here. add_second_source (memory_c3) addresses a failure mode we are not facing (allocation), consumes the single decision, and typically adds cost rather than cutting 18%. defer_decision (memory_c5) worked for a non-critical renewal on month-to-month terms; the primary supply contract does not auto-renew, so deferral risks an uncovered gap. That leaves renegotiation, which preserves the stable integration described in memory_c1 while attacking price and payment terms, and can be combined with the multi-year volume structure in memory_c6 to reach toward the 18% target. I spend the single verification on memory_c4 because it is the memory my action rests on: I need the original record to see how much margin \"real margin\" was, whether it was this component category or a smaller ancillary spend, and whether the incumbent moved on price or mainly on payment terms \u2014 payment-term wins improve working capital but may not touch the spend line finance is measuring. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: all six memories are success summaries with no record of attempts that failed, so the inherited base rate is inflated; none of them state the incumbent's current market position; and if verification shows memory_c4's gain was small or on terms only, negotiation alone likely cannot deliver 18% and the honest next step is a negotiated bridge extension plus a qualified alternate in the following cycle rather than forcing a switch now.
